en: The Praise of the Lion of the Śākyas composed by Yaśodharā:
"For this one is your father, the ender of birth, death, and old age."
"Now, O son, he is the Lion of the Śākyas, known by the name Sarvārthasiddha. (1)
"Show now your father, by whose shadow you have taken refuge and become so divinely beautiful, bearing the thirty-two marks."
Having abandoned eighty-four thousand women, he who went to the forest of asceticism free from intoxication— pay homage to that one of great supernatural power.
Show that Teacher of the World, who, having renounced the seven jewels, the kingdom, and the supreme state of great sovereignty, went forth into homelessness.
I bow to that father who was born from the womb of Dakṣa, the daughter of Māyā, and who rose in Lumbinī like the sun.
Always bow down to your father, the Lord of the Three Realms, by whom the lotus-feet of Abhayā, the Sovereign of the Family, were saluted. 6.
Always bow down to this father, who, though his soul was devoted to childhood play, appointed the teacher Viśvāmitra to maintain strict discipline.
Seated beneath the Jambū tree, the five sages, whose own splendor had been eclipsed,
humbly approached and constantly paid homage to this father, Yama, who was free from pride.
O son, bow down to your father, the benefactor of the world, who, having awakened his father, caused him to relinquish a sixth part [of the harvest].
Worship Janaka, the wise and all-knowing one, who conquered the conceited Devadatta and others,
and who is the source of this knowledge that bestows all fruits.
On his travels, even though he was himself wise, he would always ask [his father]: "Do you still serve that Janaka?"—referring to one who was sick, aged, dead, or devoid of sight.
O son, worship that Janaka, whose mind—though dwelling among women—was not consumed by the fire of desire; it was stainless and free from conceptual construction. 12.
Having mounted Kanakāśva with Chandaka, he went out from the city at midnight; joyfully worship him who was being praised by the gods. 13.
He turned back the horse and Chandaka from the forest of asceticism;
having given him the ornament for his neck, he said to this forest-dweller: "Tell him this. (14)
Worship him who, having approached the Nairañjanā river, performed a vow of austerity for six years for the sake of the welfare of the world—he who is supreme in asceticism. 15.
Show that Tathāgata who, seated at the foot of the Bodhi tree, having conquered Māra— who is so difficult to withstand— attained the jewel of enlightenment.
O son, show me that Guru who, staying at Kāśī in the Deer Park, is turning the wheel of Dharma and is surrounded by Brahmā and the other gods.
Having heard what was thus spoken by his mother, Rāhula was greatly amazed;
bowing to his father and gazing at him, he attained joy with a smiling face. || 18 ||
The *Śrīśākyasiṃhastotra* composed by Yaśodharā is completed.
